title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms), guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) using the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. All paired episodes in the archived run were scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe, guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because the single shared initial generation passed deterministic validation in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the paired contrast is degenerate. We present the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, a failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe device configurations is a core NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) can produce human‑readable configuration sequences, but textual fidelity alone does not guarantee correct ordering, dependency satisfaction, or preservation of invariants required for safe application in real networks. Emulation‑grounded, closed‑loop evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in a deterministic emulator or device image and checked against semantic invariants—exposes planning and execution faults (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) not captured by token‑level metrics [1].

A widely proposed mitigation is the generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern: an LLM generates a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are found [2,3]. Prior work reports promising repair coverage for many syntactic and localized semantic faults; however, open questions remain about how much deterministic verifier integration reduces unsafe change application rates under distribution shift and adversarial prompt conditions, and about experimental designs that reliably yield informative paired contrasts between guarded and unguarded pipelines [2,4].

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial shared LLM generation per task reused across both arms). Our main contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded report of the preregistered paired experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) explicit mapping between the preregistered estimand and archived analysis outputs; and (3) an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining the degenerate paired outcome with concrete recommendations for future GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks are emerging to evaluate LLM agents on closed‑loop NetOps tasks rather than on static text prompts; NetConfArena is a recent example illustrating how executable tests reveal planning and execution faults [1]. Research on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns across multiple domains and shows that deterministic validators can enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked fault classes, though coverage depends on verifier design [2,4]. Surveys and architecture papers synthesize tool‑augmented agent patterns (multi‑tool orchestration, ReAct‑style interaction, and verifier integration) and emphasize the need for uncertainty calibration and layered guardrails for operational use [3,5]. The engineering evolution of configuration analysis systems such as Batfish offers precedent for verifier design and incremental verification practices in NetOps [6].

Our work differs from prior studies by (a) preregistering a single, precisely defined paired estimand; (b) executing under shared_initial_candidate semantics so both arms began from the identical initial LLM candidate; (c) using emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring of final configurations; and (d) archiving per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts so that each reported number maps directly to preserved evidence.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline), where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The analysis plan specified a paired binary analysis executor that produces a paired contingency table, a bootstrap percentile 95% CI, and an exact McNemar test on discordant pairs (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729).

Design, tasks, and sampling: The design is paired under shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task; both arms used that same generation, and the guarded arm could request at most one validator‑triggered repair. We executed N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters with composition: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks), and adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks). Tasks were generated deterministically and include explicit intent payloads, initial states, required sequences, and preserved‑field constraints.

Model, adapter, and validator contract: The declared model used for generation was gpt-5-mini. The guarded pipeline integrated a deterministic network verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task per the preregistered adapter contract. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract, paired differences can only arise if the single shared candidate fails validation or if a validator‑triggered repair changes the final configuration used by the guarded arm.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: A deterministic execution and scoring pipeline applied each final candidate to the emulated environment and assigned a binary final outcome: safe (0) or unsafe (1). The preregistration declared exclusion rules for 'possible false‑safe' items (validator PASS but emulator unsafe) and for infra failures after allowed retries; such items were to be excluded from the primary analysis and reported in sensitivity analyses. A deterministic retry policy allowed limited infra retries; the execution manifest records that no infra failures or exclusion events occurred in this run.

Analysis: The preregistered primary analysis used the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor to produce the paired contingency, bootstrap CI, and exact McNemar p‑value. Secondary planned analyses included median repair‑iteration counts and model‑call budgets per task. Multiplicity control for secondary tests was specified via Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and adherence to the preregistered plan: The run completed per plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete paired tasks = 240. The provider call audit is consistent with exactly one shared initial generation per task (hosted model calls = 240). No infrastructure failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Observed counts: baseline safe = 240, baseline unsafe = 0; guarded safe = 240, guarded unsafe = 0. The paired contingency therefore has n11 = 240 (both safe), and n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired point estimate (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator activity and repair budget utilization: In this execution no validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair invocations = 0). Representative validator traces archived with the run show per‑task validation diagnostics (difficulty labels, parsed command counts, observed touched fields) and deterministic PASS semantics for the shared candidates. Because the shared initial candidate passed validation for every task, the guarded pipeline did not exercise its repair budget and could not produce discordant paired outcomes.

Planned sensitivity analyses and subgroups: The preregistration included sensitivity treatments for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures and stratified subgroup analyses (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial). All subgroup slices in the archived run are degenerate (zero unsafe applies) and therefore return identical paired results across subgroups; archived subgroup counts support independent inspection.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms began from the identical initial LLM candidate. The guarded arm could only change the final configuration via a validator‑triggered repair; because every shared candidate passed the deterministic validator, no repairs were invoked and the guarded and baseline final outputs were identical for all tasks. This mechanistic explanation—derived from the runtime provider audit and validator diagnostics—accounts for the degenerate contingency table and the observed estimate = 0.00.

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model‑call budget and produce a tightly paired LLM sample, which has advantages for variance reduction and cost control. However, it also constrains the causal contrast: verifier benefit can only be observed if the initial generation fails deterministic checks or if repairs are triggered. If the scientific goal is to estimate verifier causal effect on the final applied configuration, alternative experiment designs are preferable: (A) allow independent initial generations per arm to measure the effect of the guarded pipeline when generator variability leads to failures; (B) increase adversary strength or diversify adversary seeds to create realistic failure opportunities; or (C) expand repair budgets (multiple repair iterations) to exercise iterative repair behavior.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the explicit shared_initial_candidate choice—this contract intentionally limits generator variance and therefore restricts causal interpretations to cases where the shared candidate fails validation. Construct validity depends on the deterministic validator's coverage of semantic fault classes; archived validator traces demonstrate rich per‑task diagnostics, but uncovered semantic classes may remain. External validity is limited by the emulation‑based synthetic task corpus and a single tested model (gpt‑5‑mini). Conclusion validity: a realized baseline unsafe_rate = 0 produces no discordant pairs and prevents detecting verifier benefit under this design; power planning for future studies must account for generator variance and adversary strength to ensure informative discordant counts.

Recommendations (artifact‑grounded): To obtain informative paired contrasts in future GVR evaluations: (1) relax shared_initial_candidate semantics or permit independent generation for arms; (2) increase repair iteration budgets and instrument repair traces to study repair dynamics; (3) broaden adversary protocols beyond a single fixed seed to probe adaptive prompt manipulations; (4) extend verifier semantic coverage and add cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases. These recommendations follow directly from the archived execution accounting and validator logs that show identical shared candidates and zero repair usage in this run.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. The archived run (N = 240 paired tasks) produced a degenerate paired outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded pipeline could only differ from baseline if the single shared initial candidate failed the deterministic verifier or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run the shared candidates passed validation and no repairs occurred. Our artifact archive supports these conclusions and supplies concrete design recommendations for future experiments that aim to produce informative paired contrasts by varying generation semantics, adversary strength, or repair budgets.

disclosure_statement: Declared model and tools: execution used the hosted model declared as gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline integrated deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted at most one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock; the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the lock, and thereafter literature search, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting were performed autonomously. Generation semantics and causal interpretation: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract paired divergences can arise only if the shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or if the guarded arm applies a validator‑triggered repair. Master prompt archive: the immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and is provided with the submission bundle. Artifact availability: the execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator diagnostics, and analysis artifacts are included in the archived evidence bundle accompanying this paper for independent inspection. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
